facts.claim: Garcia-Molina and Salem (Princeton, 1987) named it a saga: a long job split into steps, where either every step finishes or compensating steps run to amend the part that did.
Garcia-Molina and Salem (1987): the steps of a saga belong together, so any half-finished run is undesirable and must be compensated for.
Garcia-Molina and Salem (1987): with save points, a crashed saga need not undo everything; the system undoes only the steps since the last save point, then restarts from there.
Garcia-Molina and Salem (1987): a saga ends either with every step done, or with the steps done so far and then their compensating steps, newest first.
Garcia-Molina and Salem (1987): a compensating step undoes a step’s meaning, not its exact state: cancel the seat booking, don’t restore yesterday’s seat count.
Garcia-Molina and Salem (1987): a sent letter can’t be taken back, so to compensate, send a second letter explaining the problem; better still, not to need it.
Garcia-Molina and Salem (1987) warn that some steps may have no compensation at all: if a step fires a missile, it may not be possible to undo it.
Garcia-Molina and Salem (1987): when a saga’s last step also ends the saga, that last step needs no compensating step at all.
Stripe’s developer docs (checked November 2026): with an idempotency key, a request that hit a connection error can be repeated without creating a second object or doing the update twice.

Stripe’s developer docs, for its original v1 requests: Stripe saves the result of the first request with a given idempotency key, and every retry with that key gets the saved result back, errors included.
Stripe’s developer docs: a key may be removed once it is at least 24 hours old, and a request reusing it after that runs again as new.
Stripe’s developer docs suggest random keys such as V4 UUIDs, up to 255 characters, and warn against using email addresses or other personal details as keys.
